result: A virtual reality (VR) system using an LCD screen at 120 fps with automated feeders successfully replicated real prey conditions for archerfish. The VR system elicited turn decisions that were statistically indistinguishable from those made with real falling objects across all measured parameters including accuracy (p=0.506), latency (p=0.297), and kinematics, with fish turning toward virtual impact points rather than feeder positions even when systematically offset.
status_reasoning: Claims C30-C37 provide comprehensive validation of the VR system through multiple control experiments and statistical comparisons. The system met all four stated requirements: appropriate temporal/spatial resolution, reward delivery without confounding cues, statistical equivalence to real conditions, and sustained motivation. Critical controls (C33-C34) demonstrated that fish responded to screen motion rather than feeders, and extensive statistical testing (C35-C37) confirmed equivalence across multiple parameters.

result: Adult archerfish successfully reprogrammed their highspeed decision-making to follow a novel non-ballistic rule where prey trajectories deflected 39.8° after initial straight movement. After 1750+ presentations over 55 days, fish accurately turned toward new deflected virtual impact points (VIPs) rather than ballistic VIPs, even when only initial straight movement was shown and feeders were offset from VIPs. The reprogrammed decisions maintained the same speed and lacked speed-accuracy tradeoff (no correlation between error and latency, p>0.1).
status_reasoning: Claims C5 and C38-C47 collectively demonstrate successful reprogramming through extensive training data, critical control experiments, and statistical analyses. The key controls (C43-C44) showing accurate performance with only initial movement visible and with offset feeders rule out alternative explanations. The absence of speed-accuracy tradeoff in reprogrammed decisions (C46) and maintenance of response characteristics (C40-C41) further support that this represents genuine decision circuit reprogramming rather than slower compensatory mechanisms.

result: After training at a single height level, archerfish immediately generalized the deflected rule to untrained height levels, prey sizes, and speeds with no initial errors or learning period. Fish accurately turned to deflected VIPs appropriate for novel conditions (all p>0.07 for difference from zero) rather than to ballistic VIPs (all p<0.001) or predictions based on training height substitution (all p<0.001), demonstrating abstract rule representation rather than lookup table learning.
status_reasoning: Claims C6 and C48-C55 provide strong evidence for immediate generalization across three independent dimensions (height, size, speed). The statistical analyses (C49-C50, C52, C54) consistently show accurate performance from the first trials at novel parameter values, ruling out gradual learning. The systematic testing against alternative predictions ('ballistic' and 'substitute') provides rigorous controls. This pattern of immediate, accurate generalization across multiple untrained dimensions strongly supports abstract rule representation.

result: Archerfish decision circuits can simultaneously operate two distinct rules based on object shape: ballistic rule for triangles and deflected rule for disks. After learning both rules (~300 additional triangle presentations), fish accurately applied the appropriate rule based on shape (p>0.07 for correct VIPs, p<0.001 for incorrect VIPs) with identical latency (p=0.189) and kinematics (p=0.984). Individual fish analysis confirmed all three top contributors could apply both rules accurately.
status_reasoning: Claims C7 and C56-C64 demonstrate dual rule usage through systematic training and testing. The critical tests (C59) showing appropriate responses when only initial straight movement was visible for both shapes, combined with statistical equivalence in timing and kinematics (C60), indicate true parallel rule implementation. Individual fish analysis (C62-C63) rules out the alternative that different fish specialized in different rules. The shape-dependent rule selection with maintained speed and accuracy represents sophisticated conditional decision-making.

result: Shape information needed for rule selection can be extracted during the brief decision phase (<100 ms) after motion onset, without requiring prior information. When shape was revealed only at motion onset (no 2 s preview), decisions remained accurate for both rules (p>0.4 for appropriate VIPs) with error distributions statistically indistinguishable from conditions with prior shape information (p=0.269).
status_reasoning: Claims C65-C67 demonstrate that rule selection occurs within the rapid decision window through direct experimental manipulation of information timing. The statistical equivalence of performance (C66) between prior information and motion-onset-only conditions provides strong evidence that shape processing and rule selection are integrated into the highspeed decision process rather than requiring preparatory processing.

result: Archerfish turn decisions are made in less than 100 ms (as little as 40 ms under optimal conditions) and lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff, yet demonstrate flexibility through learning, generalization, and dual rule operation. This challenges the assumption that highspeed decisions lacking speed-accuracy tradeoffs must rely on inflexible simplifying heuristics.
status_reasoning: Claims C8, C19, C21 establish the decision speed through current and cited measurements. Claim C46 demonstrates absence of speed-accuracy tradeoff in reprogrammed decisions. Claims C68, C74, C91 synthesize these findings with the demonstrated flexibility (from previous result groups) to support the main conclusion. The combination of speed measurements, statistical analyses of speed-accuracy relationships, and successful reprogramming/generalization experiments provides strong support for this counterintuitive finding.

result: The manuscript establishes background knowledge that speed-accuracy tradeoffs are well-documented across species (C1, C9), but some rapid decisions deviate from this pattern (C2, C10), with the prevailing explanation being use of simplifying heuristics that lack flexibility (C3, C15).
status_reasoning: Claims C1-C3, C9-C10, C15 accurately represent established knowledge in decision-making research, supported by appropriate citations (C9: Chittka et al., 2009; C10: multiple citations). These claims provide the conceptual framework and motivation for the study. The characterization of the field's understanding appears accurate based on the cited literature.

result: Male hoverflies use hardwired assumptions about female speed, size, and acceleration for rapid interception decisions, making predictable errors when challenged with objects deviating from these assumptions, exemplifying inflexible highspeed decision-making.
status_reasoning: Claims C16-C17 accurately describe cited work (Collett and Land, 1978) on hoverfly interception behavior. This serves as a comparative example of hardwired highspeed decisions. The characterization appears consistent with the cited source and provides appropriate context for contrasting with archerfish flexibility.

result: Archerfish use initial prey motion information (speed, direction, height) sampled in a brief interval after motion onset to turn toward ballistic landing points, as demonstrated by accurate turns to virtual impact points when prey was prevented from falling. This behavior has been consistently observed across lab and wild populations.
status_reasoning: Claims C4, C18, C20, C22-C27 describe established archerfish behavior from prior research, supported by multiple citations (Rossel et al., 2002; Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Reinel and Schuster, 2014, 2018a, 2018b). The glass plate experiments (C22-C23) provide key evidence that fish compute ballistic trajectories from initial motion. This well-documented baseline behavior is essential for interpreting the current study's findings.

result: The authors initially hypothesized that archerfish decisions would be hardwired to ballistics, either genetically or through early ontogeny, based on the consistent ballistic responses observed across all previous studies.
status_reasoning: Claims C28-C29 explicitly state the authors' initial hypothesis and reasoning. This is appropriately labeled as speculation (C28) and represents a reasonable hypothesis given the prior evidence (C27). The hypothesis provides clear motivation for the experimental approach and is later refuted by the experimental findings.

result: The cognitive aspects demonstrated in archerfish (generalization, shape recognition, rule learning) are not unique to this species but have been documented in other animals including those with smaller brains. What is novel is finding these capacities in decisions made at reflex-like speed (<100 ms), with the task complexity comparable to sophisticated laboratory tasks requiring conditional rule switching.
status_reasoning: Claims C70-C73 appropriately contextualize the findings within broader comparative cognition literature, supported by relevant citations. Claims C75-C76 make reasonable comparisons to laboratory tasks. Claims C77-C80 accurately represent research on cognition in smaller brains. The synthesis (C70, C74) correctly identifies that the novelty lies in the combination of speed and cognitive sophistication rather than the cognitive capacities per se.

result: Archerfish turn decisions use C-start motor patterns equivalent to escape responses, among the fastest C-starts in fish, with motor circuits restricted to hindbrain networks organized around the Mauthner neuron, though additional hindbrain neurons are needed for precision.
status_reasoning: Claims C81-C84 accurately describe the neural and motor basis of archerfish turns based on cited research (Wöhl and Schuster, 2007; Korn and Faber, 2005; Machnik et al., 2018a, 2018b; Hecker et al., 2020). This provides important context about the neural constraints on the decision system and supports the characterization of these as highspeed decisions implemented by relatively small neural circuits.

result: The authors propose that decision flexibility evolved due to ecological pressures: severe competition from other surface-feeding fish and need to handle prey of varying sizes that fall with different trajectories due to air resistance. Hardwired ballistic-only responses would produce errors for larger prey requiring time-costly corrections.
status_reasoning: Claims C85-C90 present ecological and evolutionary explanations for the observed flexibility. While C85 and C87 are supported by citations and physics, the evolutionary explanation (C86, C90) is explicitly speculative ('we suggest, clearly without proof'). Claims C88-C89 involve logical inferences about adaptive advantages. The ecological context is plausible and the reasoning is sound, but these remain untested hypotheses rather than demonstrated facts. The authors appropriately label these as speculative.

result: The findings raise questions about whether similar flexibility exists in other highspeed decisions and suggest potential technological applications for rapid yet flexible decision-making systems.
status_reasoning: Claims C92-C93 appropriately identify future research directions and potential applications based on the demonstrated findings. These are reasonable extrapolations labeled as speculative. They do not overstate the implications and appropriately frame these as possibilities rather than established facts.

result: The study used six adult archerfish with standardized visual stimuli (Michelson contrast 0.96), ballistic motion parameters (1.775 m/s horizontal speed, 243 ms to virtual landing), bottom-view recording, and group competition conditions required for eliciting start decisions.
status_reasoning: Claims C94-C98 describe methodological details that are straightforward factual statements about the experimental setup. These are appropriately documented and provide necessary information for evaluating and replicating the study. The requirement for group competition (C98) is supported by citation.

result: Examples of rapid decisions lacking speed-accuracy tradeoffs include: rats categorizing odors in one sniff (~300 ms) with no improvement from additional time, archerfish turns showing no latency-accuracy correlation, humans classifying images in 20-40 ms, and baseball hitters making bat placement decisions based on ~70 ms of visual processing.
status_reasoning: Claims C11-C14 accurately represent cited research on rapid decisions across species. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations (Uchida et al., 2006; Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; VanRullen and Thorpe, 2001 and others; Higuchi et al., 2016 and others). These examples provide important comparative context for the archerfish study and establish that rapid decisions without speed-accuracy tradeoffs are documented across diverse systems.
